title: Judges opens “after the death of Joshua”, then tells of Joshua sending the people away and dying — in what order did these things happen?
summary: The first verse of Judges dates what follows “after the death of Joshua”. A chapter later Joshua lets the people go and his death is reported. One event of chapter 1, the taking of Kirjathsepher by Othniel, is also told in Joshua 15 in almost the same words. The verses compared do not say which of these events came before Joshua’s death and which after.
text: KJV Judges 1:1: “Now after the death of Joshua it came to pass, that the children of Israel asked the Lord, saying, Who shall go up for us against the Canaanites first, to fight against them?” KJV 1:11: “And from thence he went against the inhabitants of Debir: and the name of Debir before was Kirjathsepher:” KJV 1:12: “And Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjathsepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.” KJV 1:13: “took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife” KJV 2:6: “And when Joshua had let the people go, the children of Israel went every man unto his inheritance to possess the land.” KJV 2:7: “And the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that outlived Joshua” KJV 2:8: “And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, being an hundred and ten years old.” KJV Joshua 15:13: “And unto Caleb the son of Jephunneh he gave a part among the children of Judah, according to the commandment of the Lord to Joshua” KJV Joshua 15:15: “And he went up thence to the inhabitants of Debir: and the name of Debir before was Kirjathsepher.” KJV Joshua 15:16: “And Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjathsepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.” KJV Joshua 15:17: “took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife” KJV Joshua 24:28: “So Joshua let the people depart, every man unto his inheritance.” KJV Joshua 24:29: “And it came to pass after these things, that Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, being an hundred and ten years old.” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 1:1: וַיְהִ֗י אַחֲרֵי֙ מֹ֣ות יְהֹושֻׁ֔עַ [and it came to pass after the death of Joshua]. 2:6: וַיְשַׁלַּ֥ח יְהֹושֻׁ֖עַ אֶת־הָעָ֑ם [and Joshua sent the people away]. 2:8: וַיָּ֛מָת יְהֹושֻׁ֥עַ בִּן־נ֖וּן עֶ֣בֶד יְהוָ֑ה [and Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 1:1: ἐγένετο μετὰ τὴν τελευτὴν Ἰησοῦ [it came to pass after the death of Joshua]. 2:6: Καὶ ἐξαπέστειλεν Ἰησοῦς τὸν λαὸν [and Joshua sent the people away]. 2:8: Καὶ ἐτελεύτησεν Ἰησοῦς υἱὸς Ναυῆ δοῦλος Κυρίου [and Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/1/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG01.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG02.htm.
reasoning: The opening words give a time for what follows, and the question Israel asks in the same verse leads into the campaigns of chapter 1. Yet 2:6–8 has Joshua alive, dismissing the people, and then dying, in words close to Joshua 24:28–29; and the taking of Kirjathsepher with the gift of Achsah stands both here and in Joshua 15:15–17, where it follows a grant to Caleb made “according to the commandment of the Lord to Joshua”. The order matters for reading chapter 1: it decides whether those campaigns are new wars fought after Joshua or a second telling of wars from his time, and so how they sit beside the conquest summaries in Joshua.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the verses quoted state: that Judges 1:1 is a heading for the book and chapter 1 gathers events of different times, some from Joshua’s lifetime; that everything in chapter 1 happened after Joshua’s death and Joshua 15:15–17 tells in advance of a later event; that Judges 2:6–10 goes back in time and takes up the end of the book of Joshua before the story moves on. Limits: the place of an account in a book does not by itself date it, in Joshua 15 no more than in Judges 1; the two tellings of Kirjathsepher may be one event told twice, and the verses quoted do not say so; Judges 2:6 has no word such as “had” in the Hebrew or the Greek quoted, where the KJV prints “when Joshua had let the people go”, and that difference is noted and not examined here. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “death of Joshua” finds Judges 1:1 only; Judges 1:1, 1:10–13, 1:20, 2:6–10, Joshua 15:13–17 and Joshua 24:28–31 were read in the KJV. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle the order. No H or G is proposed. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. title: What was the ephod Gideon made of the gold, and what did Israel do when it “went thither a whoring after it”?
summary: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the spoil, makes “an ephod thereof” and puts it in his city, and all Israel goes “a whoring after it”. In the other verses compared an ephod is a thing a priest wears or brings. The passage does not say what Gideon’s ephod was, what it was for, or what the people did with it.
text: KJV Judges 8:23: “I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you” KJV 8:24: “I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey” KJV 8:26: “And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold” KJV 8:27: “And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.” KJV 8:33: “as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim” KJV 17:5: “And the man Micah had an house of gods, and made an ephod, and teraphim” KJV Exodus 28:4: “And these are the garments which they shall make; a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe” KJV Exodus 28:6: “And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue, and of purple, of scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cunning work.” KJV 1 Samuel 2:18: “girded with a linen ephod” KJV 1 Samuel 23:9: “he said to Abiathar the priest, Bring hither the ephod” KJV Hosea 3:4: “without an image, and without an ephod, and without teraphim” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 8:27: וַיַּעַשׂ֩ אֹותֹ֨ו גִדְעֹ֜ון לְאֵפֹ֗וד וַיַּצֵּ֨ג אֹותֹ֤ו בְעִירֹו֙ בְּעָפְרָ֔ה וַיִּזְנ֧וּ כָֽל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אַחֲרָ֖יו שָׁ֑ם [and Gideon made it into an ephod and set it in his city, in Ophrah, and all Israel went whoring after it there]. Exodus 28:6: וְעָשׂ֖וּ אֶת־הָאֵפֹ֑ד [and they shall make the ephod]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 8:27: Καὶ ἐποίησεν αὐτὸ Γεδεὼν εἰς ἐφὼδ, καὶ ἔστησεν αὐτὸ ἐν πόλει αὐτοῦ ἐν Ἐφραθά [and Gideon made it into an ephod and set it up in his city, in Ephratha]. Exodus 28:6: Καὶ ποιήσουσι τὴν ἐπωμίδα [and they shall make the shoulder-piece]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/8/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/28/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG08.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO28.htm.
reasoning: In the verses compared outside Judges an ephod is listed among garments, is worn (“girded with a linen ephod”), or is brought by a priest when David wants to enquire. Gideon’s is made out of gold weighed at seventeen hundred shekels, is “put” in a town, and draws “all Israel”. The passage gives the result, a snare to Gideon and his house, without saying what the object was or what the people did. That bears on what Gideon is being charged with, straight after he has said “the Lord shall rule over you”: making an idol, or setting up a means of enquiry or of priestly service away from the sanctuary.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that it was a priestly garment heavy with gold, kept at Ophrah and used to enquire of God; that it was an image, or the covering of an image, which the people worshipped; that it was a trophy of the victory that came to be treated as holy. Limits: the phrase “went a whoring after” is used six verses later of the Baalim, which shows the phrase can be used of other gods and does not show what was done at Ophrah; Micah’s ephod at Judges 17:5 stands beside teraphim in “an house of gods” and Hosea 3:4 lists an ephod with an image and teraphim, but being named together does not make the things alike; the weight given is that of the earrings asked for, and the verse does not say that all of it went into the ephod. Brenton’s Greek keeps the Hebrew word as a name at Judges 8:27 and has a Greek word for a shoulder-piece at Exodus 28:6; that is a difference within the Greek edition and settles nothing about the object. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV of Judges for “ephod” finds 8:27, 17:5, 18:14, 18:17, 18:18 and 18:20; the other verses quoted were chosen from a search of 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel and Hosea for the same word. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what Gideon’s ephod was. No H or G is proposed. title: What was the “evil spirit” God sent between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, and how did it work?
summary: After three years of Abimelech’s rule “God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem”, and the men of Shechem turn on him. The next verse gives the purpose: the blood of Gideon’s sons is to come upon both. The passage does not say what the evil spirit was or how it brought the treachery about.
text: KJV Judges 9:22: “When Abimelech had reigned three years over Israel,” KJV 9:23: “Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech:” KJV 9:24: “That the cruelty done to the threescore and ten sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid upon Abimelech their brother” KJV 9:25: “And the men of Shechem set liers in wait for him in the top of the mountains” KJV 9:56: “Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech” KJV 9:57: “And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads” KJV 1 Samuel 16:14: “But the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him.” KJV 1 Kings 22:21: “And there came forth a spirit, and stood before the Lord, and said, I will persuade him.” KJV 1 Kings 22:22: “I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” KJV Numbers 5:14: “the spirit of jealousy come upon him” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 9:23: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֱלֹהִים֙ ר֣וּחַ רָעָ֔ה בֵּ֣ין אֲבִימֶ֔לֶךְ וּבֵ֖ין בַּעֲלֵ֣י שְׁכֶ֑ם [and God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the lords of Shechem]. 1 Samuel 16:14: רֽוּחַ־רָעָ֖ה מֵאֵ֥ת יְהוָֽה [an evil spirit from the LORD]. 1 Kings 22:22: ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר [a spirit of falsehood]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 9:23: Καὶ ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ Θεὸς πνεῦμα πονηρὸν ἀναμέσον Ἀβιμέλεχ καὶ ἀναμέσον τῶν ἀνδρῶν Σικίμων [and God sent out an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem]. 1 Samuel 16:14: πνεῦμα πονηρὸν παρὰ Κυρίου [an evil spirit from the Lord]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/9/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/9/16/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/22/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG09.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/1SA16.htm.
reasoning: The verse makes God the sender of something it calls evil, and puts the men’s treachery next. What follows in the story is told as ordinary human action: ambushes in the mountains, a newcomer the men trust, a battle. Whether the “evil spirit” is a being that God dispatched or a name for the ill will that arose decides how the passage relates God’s act to the men’s own guilt, which 9:56–57 goes on to say God repaid on their heads.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that a spirit being was sent, as 1 Kings 22:21–22 tells of a spirit that stands before the Lord and offers to go; that “spirit” here means a temper or disposition of hostility, as the KJV speaks of “the spirit of jealousy” at Numbers 5:14; that the words are the narrator’s way of saying that God was behind a quarrel which arose by ordinary causes. Limits: the same two Hebrew words stand at 1 Samuel 16:14, but a shared phrase does not settle that the same thing is meant in a different story, and that verse does not say what the spirit is either; 1 Kings 22 is a vision told by a prophet and says nothing of Shechem; “evil” in the phrase may describe what the spirit brings, harm, and need not describe its moral nature, and the passage does not say which. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “evil spirit” and “evil spirits” finds Judges 9:23; 1 Samuel 16:14, 16:15, 16:16, 16:23, 18:10 and 19:9; Luke 7:21 and 8:2; Acts 19:12, 19:13, 19:15 and 19:16. Of these only Judges 9:23 and 1 Samuel 16:14 were read here, with Judges 9:22–26 and 9:56–57. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what the evil spirit was. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Jephthah “did with her according to his vow” — what was done to his daughter?
summary: Jephthah vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him “shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering”. His only child comes out. After two months she returns and he “did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man”. The passage does not describe the act.
text: KJV Judges 11:30: “And Jephthah vowed a vow unto the Lord” KJV 11:31: “Then it shall be, that whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.” KJV 11:34: “his daughter came out to meet him with timbrels and with dances: and she was his only child” KJV 11:35: “for I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back” KJV 11:37: “let me alone two months, that I may go up and down upon the mountains, and bewail my virginity” KJV 11:38: “and bewailed her virginity upon the mountains” KJV 11:39: “And it came to pass at the end of two months, that she returned unto her father, who did with her according to his vow which he had vowed: and she knew no man. And it was a custom in Israel,” KJV 11:40: “That the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in a year.” KJV Deuteronomy 12:31: “for even their sons and their daughters they have burnt in the fire to their gods” KJV 1 Samuel 12:11: “And the Lord sent Jerubbaal, and Bedan, and Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you” KJV Hebrews 11:32: “for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae” Hebrew (WLC) Judges 11:31: וְהָיָה֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה וְהַעֲלִיתִ֖הוּ עֹולָֽה [and it shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering]. 11:39: וַיַּ֣עַשׂ לָ֔הּ אֶת־נִדְרֹ֖ו אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָדָ֑ר וְהִיא֙ לֹא־יָדְעָ֣ה אִ֔ישׁ [and he did to her his vow which he had vowed; and she had not known a man]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Judges 11:31: καὶ ἔσται τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἀνοίσω αὐτὸν ὁλοκαύτωμα [and he shall be the Lord's; I will offer him up as a whole burnt offering]. 11:39: καὶ ἐποίησεν ἐν αὐτῇ τὴν εὐχὴν αὐτοῦ ἣν ηὔξατο· καὶ αὕτη οὐκ ἔγνω ἄνδρα [and he performed on her his vow which he had vowed; and she knew no man]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/11/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG11.htm.
reasoning: The vow names a burnt offering, and the fulfilment is told in seven English words that point back to the vow without repeating it. What the passage dwells on instead is her virginity: she asks two months to bewail it, and the report of the fulfilment is followed at once by “and she knew no man”. Whether a judge of Israel burnt his daughter to the Lord, or did something else that the vow’s words could cover, is the weightiest fact of the story and the one the passage leaves untold. The verses compared pass no judgement on the act either way.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that Jephthah offered his daughter as a burnt offering, as the words of the vow say; that he gave her to the Lord to live unmarried, a reading that points to the mourning of her virginity and not of her death and to “and she knew no man” after the fulfilment; that the vow had two parts, one for a person and one for a beast, a reading that depends on how the joining word in 11:31 is taken. Limits: the KJV’s “according to” is not a separate word in the Hebrew or the Greek quoted, which say that he did, or performed, his vow to her; “she knew no man” can be read as what followed from the vow or as a statement of her condition when it was carried out, and the passage does not say which; Deuteronomy 12:31 calls the burning of sons and daughters a thing the nations did to their gods and is quoted as a text used in this debate, not as an account of what Jephthah did; 1 Samuel 12:11 and Hebrews 11:32 name Jephthah without mentioning the vow or the daughter. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “Jephthah” and “Jephthae” outside Judges finds 1 Samuel 12:11 and Hebrews 11:32 only; Judges 11:29–40 was read in the KJV, and 11:30–31 and 11:34–40 also in the Hebrew and the Greek. That is a word search and a reading of those verses, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what was done. No H, G or V is proposed.
